assertions.description: createElement returns an element for any name that is a valid element name, whether or not the browser has ever heard of it. A truthiness check on the result therefore cannot detect this removal, or any other — which is the mistake this feature's migration page exists to head off.

The end state of the removal, demonstrated on a tag no browser has ever implemented: an element name that is not registered produces an HTMLUnknownElement, which has none of the removed element's properties. This is what fencedframe becomes.
assertions.test: (()=>{try{const el=document.createElement('bananaframe');return el instanceof HTMLUnknownElement&&!('config' in el);}catch(e){return false;}})()

assertions.description: The interface object and the config property are removed together, so a page may test for either and get the same answer. Holds on both sides of the removal: both true while the element exists, both false once it does not.

FencedFrameConfig has no constructor exposed to pages: a config may only be produced by an auction or by Shared Storage. This is why removing those producers is sufficient to make the element unusable, and it holds vacuously once the interface itself is gone.
assertions.test: (()=>{try{if(typeof FencedFrameConfig!=='function')return true;try{new FencedFrameConfig('https://example.com');return false;}catch(e){return e instanceof TypeError;}}catch(e){return false;}})()
